passage: Dear Tushar, Thank you for helping with the science project last week. I have been thinking about the day we took the bus to the lab. You had to leave home at five to get there on time, and you mentioned it as if it was nothing. I get dropped by car, and I have never once wondered how I would get anywhere. I also realised that I have had a tutor since class six and a quiet room at home, and I always thought that was just normal for everybody. I don't feel bad, exactly. I feel more awake, and more thankful. I would like to be fairer. Next time I could help with the lab report, and share my old notebooks if you find them useful. Only if you want to. Nirmala

qa.q: At what time did Tushar leave home to reach the lab?
qa.a: Tushar had to leave home at five to get there on time.

qa.q: How does Nirmala feel about this realisation?
qa.a: Nirmala feels more awake and thankful, not guilty. Nirmala says "I don't feel bad, exactly" and wants to be fairer.

qa.q: What choice does Nirmala make in the letter after seeing the difference?
qa.a: Nirmala offers to help with the lab report and share old notebooks, but only if Tushar wants, so the offer stays respectful.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel on receiving the letter?
qa.a: Possibly surprised, and pleased to be noticed. Because the offer is optional, Tushar can accept it without feeling pitied. 🙂

grounding: A teenager from a comfortable background notices advantages that others lack, feels thankfulness rather than guilt, and wants to act fairly.

passage: So on the school radio show they asked, what changed how you see things this year? For me it was Afreen. She topped the maths test, and I asked if she wanted to revise at my place, and she said she had to catch the six-ten bus, because there's no later one. I had always thought everyone had a fan, a desk and a quiet corner. Afreen does her homework on a shared table with her little brothers. That day I realised that my marks come partly from my things. I don't think that's something to feel guilty about. It just means I should say thank you at home, and make sure Afreen gets the same practice papers I get. We share them now, and she explains the tricky ones better than my tutor does. Shankar

qa.q: What bus did Afreen have to catch?
qa.a: Afreen had to catch the six-ten bus, because there is no later one.

qa.q: What did Shankar realise that day, and how does Shankar feel about it?
qa.a: Shankar realised that the marks come partly from having a fan, a desk and a quiet corner. Shankar feels thankful and more aware, not guilty.

qa.q: Which choice did Shankar make after realising this?
qa.a: Shankar decided to say thank you at home and to share the same practice papers with Afreen, so both have equal practice.

qa.q: How might Afreen see the sharing of practice papers?
qa.a: Afreen probably sees it as fair and friendly, since she also explains the tricky ones and helps in return, so it is exchange and not charity.

grounding: A teenager from a comfortable background sees that ease comes with advantages others lack, and responds with thanks and fairness instead of guilt.

passage:
Last summer I didn't notice Yogesh-bhaiya at all. That's the honest truth.
He drove me to tuition every day in our car, waited in the heat for two hours, and drove me back. I was sixteen. I sat in the back seat on my phone and complained about the traffic.
Then one day my phone died and I actually looked at him. His shirt was soaked. He was eating dry rotis from a steel box on his lap, in the driver's seat, because there was nowhere else to go.
I asked, "Don't you get lunch?"
He said, "This is lunch, Shreya beti."
I didn't feel guilty exactly. I felt like someone had turned on a light. I talked to Papa that night, and now Bhaiya waits in the tuition centre's canteen, and I ask about his daughter's school.

qa.q: Where did Yogesh-bhaiya eat his rotis?
qa.a: He ate dry rotis from a steel box on his lap, in the driver's seat.

qa.q: How did Shreya feel when she finally looked at Yogesh-bhaiya?
qa.a: Shreya felt surprised and thoughtful, like someone had turned on a light, more aware than guilty.

qa.q: What small step did Shreya take, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Shreya talked to Papa so Yogesh-bhaiya could wait in the canteen, and began asking about his daughter; seeing her advantages led to fairer treatment and thankfulness.

qa.q: What might it be like for Yogesh-bhaiya to wait in the heat every day?
qa.a: It is probably tiring and uncomfortable, and he may feel unseen by the family he drives for.

grounding: A teenager from a comfortable background notices advantages she had taken for granted, and responds with fairness rather than guilt.

passage:
Football coach's note, under-16 girls, Saturday.
Before practice, Madhuri complained loudly that Reena "never has proper boots" and was "slowing the team down." She said, "Why can't she just buy some? They're not that expensive."
Reena heard. She laced her torn canvas shoes and said nothing.
After practice I asked Madhuri to help me carry the cones. I asked her how she got to practice. "Mum drops me." And Reena? Madhuri didn't know. I told her: two buses and a walk, after helping at her family's tea stall.
Madhuri was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "I didn't think about it. I thought everyone had what I have."
I told her that noticing is the point, not feeling bad. Next step: I will ask the club about a boots fund, and Madhuri has asked if she can help organise it.

qa.q: How does Reena get to practice?
qa.a: Two buses and a walk, after helping at her family's tea stall.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when she said she thought everyone had what she has?
qa.a: Madhuri felt surprised and a little embarrassed, realising she had not noticed her own advantages.

qa.q: What did the coach do that helped Madhuri learn?
qa.a: The coach spoke to her privately, asked simple questions, shared Reena's reality, and said noticing matters more than feeling bad.

qa.q: How might Reena feel when Madhuri complains about her boots?
qa.a: Reena probably felt humiliated and hurt, lacing her torn shoes silently while being blamed for slowing the team.

grounding: A coach's note shows a teenager from an easier background learning to see her advantages without guilt, and turning toward fairness.

passage:
Tuesday
Group project due Friday. Vishal hasn't sent his slides AGAIN. I messaged the group, "Some people don't care." He left the chat.
Then at break, Vishal told me he doesn't have a laptop. He does his part on his uncle's phone after he closes the shop at nine. He said it without looking at me.
I felt stupid. I have a laptop, a desk, Wi-Fi, and Mum brings me tea while I work. I just thought that was normal. I never thought of it as having something.
I don't want to feel guilty forever. That won't help Vishal. So I asked if he wants to work at my place tomorrow after school. He said yes. And I apologised in the group chat.
Bhupen

qa.q: When does Vishal do his part of the project?
qa.a: He does his part on his uncle's phone after he closes the shop at nine.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling after Vishal explained?
qa.a: Bhupen felt stupid and a bit guilty, realising that a laptop, Wi-Fi and a quiet desk were advantages, not just normal.

qa.q: What did Bhupen do that turned the feeling into fairness?
qa.a: Bhupen invited Vishal to work at Bhupen's place and apologised in the group chat, instead of staying stuck in guilt.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt when Bhupen wrote "Some people don't care"?
qa.a: Vishal likely felt hurt and embarrassed, since he was working hard late at night and was blamed in front of everyone.

grounding: A teenager realises that ease taken for granted is an advantage a classmate lacks, and responds with fairness and thanks rather than guilt.

passage:
Vidya: coming to the robotics camp in May? 😊 everyone's going
Nitin: nope
Vidya: why?? you're the best in class at this
Nitin: it's 3 weeks. I help at the shop in May. and no laptop at home, remember
Vidya: oh. I just thought everyone had one
Vidya: sorry, that was a silly thing to say
Nitin: it's ok. you didn't know
Vidya: honestly I've never had to think about it. my dad just pays for stuff
Nitin: yeah. must be nice 🙂
Vidya: it is. I'm lucky and I should say thanks more. also the school library lends laptops for the camp, Ms. Rao told me. want to ask her together tomorrow?
Nitin: ...ok. if it's free, yes
Vidya: it's free. 8:30 at the staff room

qa.q: Why can't Nitin join the camp in May?
qa.a: Nitin helps at the shop in May and has no laptop at home.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling after typing 'I just thought everyone had one'?
qa.a: Vidya felt embarrassed and a bit ashamed, which is why the apology comes straight after.

qa.q: Which of Vidya's replies turned the moment toward fairness?
qa.a: Instead of sinking into guilt, Vidya admitted the advantage, felt thankful for it and found a practical fix: asking about the library laptops together.

qa.q: How might Nitin have felt reading Vidya's first 'why??'
qa.a: Nitin may have felt tired of explaining and a little stung that the gap went unnoticed, which shows in the short 'nope' and the dry 'must be nice'.

grounding: It illustrates a comfortable teenager noticing an unseen advantage and turning it into thankfulness and a fair practical step rather than guilt.
